cases.question: What is a principal stratum strategy for intercurrent events?

statements.text: Principal stratification is a classification of subjects according to the potential occurrence of an intercurrent event on all treatments.

citations.quote: Principal Stratification: Classification of subjects according to the potential occurrence of an intercurrent event on all treatments.

statements.text: A principal stratum strategy relates to defining the target population as the principal stratum in which an intercurrent event would (or would not) occur, so the clinical question of interest concerns the treatment effect only within that principal stratum.

citations.quote: Principal stratum strategies This relates to the population of interest (see A.3.3.). The target population might be taken to be the “ principal stratum” (see Glossary) in which an intercurrent event would occur . Alternatively, the target population might be taken to be the principal stratum in which an intercurrent event would not occur. The clinical question of interest relates to the treatment effect only within the principal stratum.

statements.text: Principal stratification should be distinguished from subsetting on actual intercurrent events because the subset who experience an intercurrent event on one treatment will often differ from the subset on the other treatment and comparing these subsets can confound treatment effects with differences in subject characteristics.

citations.quote: It is important to distinguish “ principal stratification ” (see Glossary) , which is based on potential intercurrent events (for example, subjects who would discontinue therapy if assigned to the test product), from subsetting based on actual inte rcurrent events (subjects who discontinue therapy on their assigned treatment). The subset of subjects who experience an intercurrent event on the test treatment will often be a different subset from those who experience the same intercurrent event on con trol. T reatment effects defined by comparing outcomes in these subsets confound the effects of the different treatments with the differences in outcomes possibly due to the differing characteristics of the subjects.

citations.quote: Consider an intercurrent event of discontinuation of treatment; it is of utmost importance to distinguish between treatment effects of interest based on the principal stratum of patients who would be able to continue if administered the test treatment and the effect during continued treatment. statements.text: The estimand attribute 'population' may be represented by a principal stratum defined by the occurrence (or non-occurrence) of a specific intercurrent event when constructing an estimand.

cases.question: What happens to statistical power when a drug must show an effect on each of two co-primary endpoints?

statements.text: Requiring a drug to show an effect on each of two co-primary endpoints "will increase the Type II error rate and decrease study power."

citations.quote: Using two or more endpoints for which demonstration of an effect on each is recommended to support regulatory approval (called co-primary endpoints; see section III.C.1. below) will increase the Type II error rate and decrease study power.

statements.text: If each endpoint is powered at 80% and the endpoints are independent, the power to show success on both is approximately 64% and the Type II error rate would be 36%.

citations.quote: For example, assume two endpoints have the same effect size and the study sample size is selected to provide 80% power to show success on each of these two endpoints. If the endpoints are independent, the power to show success on both will be approximately 64% (0.8 x 0.8); i.e., the likelihood of the study failing to support a conclusion of a favorable drug effect when such an effect existed (the Type II error rate) would be 36%.

statements.text: To maintain desired study power when using co-primary endpoints, the sample size should be increased and "the individual endpoints could be powered at approximately 90% to ensure the probability of success is at least 80%."

citations.quote: To maintain desired study power, a larger sample size is recommended, and the individual endpoints could be powered at approximately 90% to ensure the probability of success is at least 80%.

statements.text: Because dividing the total α equally for two endpoints gives a critical α of two-sided 0.025 for each, multiplicity control can further reduce the per-endpoint α and hence affect power.

citations.quote: The most common form of the Bonferroni method divides the available total α (typically 0.05 two-sided) equally among the chosen endpoints. ... Thus, with two endpoints, the critical α for each endpoint is two-sided 0.025.

statements.text: The guidance notes in general that "co-primary endpoint testing increases the Type II error rate" and that using more than two co-primary endpoints should be carefully considered because of the loss of power.

citations.quote: As discussed in section III.B., there is no multiplicity problem when the study is designed to demonstrate efficacy on all of the separate endpoints. However, co-primary endpoint testing increases the Type II error rate. In general, unless clinically very important, the use of more than two co-primary endpoints should be carefully considered because of the loss of power.

cases.question: According to the CPMP points to consider, what should be done when an unforeseen multiple testing situation arises?

statements.text: If a multiple test situation occurs which was not foreseen, a conservative approach will be necessary (for example Bonferroni or a related procedure).

citations.quote: If a multiple test situation occurs which was not foreseen, a conservative approach will be necessary e.g. Bonferroni’s or a related procedure.

statements.text: A conservative approach to an unforeseen multiple testing situation will inherently involve a loss of power.

citations.quote: Inherently there will be a loss of power.

statements.text: When a multiple test situation is foreseen, pre‑specification of the method used to deal with this is recommended.

citations.quote: Therefore if a multiple test situation is fore seen pre-specification of the method use to deal with this is recommended

cases.question: How do stratified randomisation and covariate adjustment relate, in the EMA guideline on baseline covariates?

statements.text: Stratified randomisation is used to reduce the likelihood of imbalances between treatment groups within levels of specified covariates and can enhance credibility and efficiency of treatment effect estimation.

citations.quote: Stratified randomisation is often used to reduce the likelihood of such imbalances between treatment groups within the levels of specified covariates (generally qualitative covariates or categorised quantitative covariates).
Balance of treatment groups with respect to one or more specific prognostic covariates can enhance the credibility of the results of the trial.
Stratification might improve the efficiency of the estimation of the treatment effect, especially for small or even moderately sized trials.

statements.text: Stratification at randomisation and adjustment for covariates in the analysis may be seen as complementary methods of accounting for covariates.

citations.quote: Stratification at the stage of randomisation and adjustment for covariates in the analysis may be seen as complementary methods of accounting for covariates.

statements.text: The primary analysis should reflect the restriction on the randomisation implied by stratification, so stratification variables (if not solely administrative) should usually be included as covariates or stratification variables in the primary analysis.

citations.quote: The primary analysis should reflect the restriction on the randomisation implied by the stratification.

For this reason, stratification variables, if not solely used for administrative reasons, should usually be included as covariates or stratification variables in the primary analysis regardless of their prognostic value.

statements.text: If stratification was done purely for an administrative reason it need not be included as a covariate in the primary model; otherwise stratification factors should normally be included as covariates in the primary outcome model.

citations.quote: The factors that are the basis of stratification should normally be included as covariates or stratification variables in the primary outcome model, except where stratification was done purely for an administrative reason.

statements.text: Covariates to be included in the primary analysis must be pre-specified in the protocol.

citations.quote: Covariates to be included in the primary analysis must be pre-specified in the protocol.

statements.text: A baseline covariate is measured or observed before randomisation and variables measured after randomisation should not be included as covariates in the primary analysis.

citations.quote: A baseline covariate in the context of this guideline is defined as a qualitative factor or a quantitative variable measured or observed before randomisation and expected to influence the primary outcome variable to be analysed.
Variables measured after randomisation and so potentially affected by the treatment should not be included as covariates in the primary analysis.

statements.text: Stratification can become impractical when there are many influential covariates or covariates with many strata, and limitations should be placed on the number of covariates included in the statistical model.

citations.quote: Stratification can become overwhelming if there are many influential covariates or covariates with many strata in the trial.
No more than a few covariates should be included in the primary analysis.
Limitations should be placed on the number of covariates included in the statistical model and on the total number of parameters.

statements.text: In multicentre trials, stratification variables used for randomisation (such as centre) should be adjusted for in the primary analysis, but adjusting for many small centres may raise analytical problems and require justification or sensitivity analyses.

citations.quote: The stratification variables used for randomisation should be adjusted for in the primary analysis.
If centre was used for stratification in a multicentre trial problems might arise in case of many centres recruiting small numbers of patients ('small centres').

If an applicant chooses not to include centre in the analysis when it was included in the randomisation scheme, they should explain why and demonstrate through sensitivity analyses that the trial conclusions are not substantially affected because of this.

statements.text: When some imbalance between treatment groups in a baseline covariate is due to chance, adjusted treatment effects may account for this imbalance and sensitivity analyses should be provided to show robustness.

citations.quote: When there is some imbalance between the treatment groups in a baseline covariate that is solely due to chance then adjusted treatment effects may account for this observed imbalance when unadjusted analyses may not.
Sensitivity analyses should be provided to demonstrate that any observed positive treatment effect is not solely explained by imbalances at baseline in any of the covariates.

statements.text: Dynamic allocation methods may be used when stratification by many factors is not possible, but their implications for bias and Type I error control should be carefully considered and re-randomisation methods in the analysis considered where appropriate.

citations.quote: techniques of dynamic allocation are sometimes used to achieve balance across several factors simultaneously.

Possible implications of dynamic allocation methods on the analysis e.g. with regard to bias and Type I error control should be carefully considered... To properly account for such problems the use of re-randomisation methods in the analysis should be considered.

cases.question: Which reference points should the starting dose of a first-in-human trial in healthy volunteers be based on in the EU?

statements.text: The starting dose for healthy volunteers should be related to the NOAEL.

citations.quote: the starting dose should either be related to the MABEL, PAD or NOAEL.

statements.text: The starting dose for healthy volunteers should be related to the MABEL (minimal anticipated biological effect level).

citations.quote: the starting dose should either be related to the MABEL, PAD or NOAEL.

Exposure showing PD effects in the non-clinical pharmacology studies, including ex vivo and in vitro studies in human tissues if feasible, should also be determined and these data should be used to determine the minimal anticipated biological effect level (MABEL) in humans and an estimation of the pharmacologically active dose (PAD) and/or anticipated therapeutic dose range (ATD) in humans.

statements.text: The starting dose for healthy volunteers should be related to the PAD (pharmacologically active dose) or ATD (anticipated therapeutic dose range) when appropriate.

citations.quote: the starting dose should either be related to the MABEL, PAD or NOAEL.

Exposure showing PD effects in the non-clinical pharmacology studies, including ex vivo and in vitro studies in human tissues if feasible, should also be determined and these data should be used to determine the minimal anticipated biological effect level (MABEL) in humans and an estimation of the pharmacologically active dose (PAD) and/or anticipated therapeutic dose range (ATD) in humans.

statements.text: The starting dose for healthy volunteers should be a dose expected to result in an exposure lower than the PAD unless a robust scientific rationale can be provided for a higher dose.

citations.quote: The starting dose for healthy volunteers should be a dose expected to result in an exposure lower than the PAD, unless a robust scientific rationale can be provided for a higher dose.

statements.text: Safety factors should generally be applied when calculating the starting dose, taking into account factors such as novelty, pharmacodynamic characteristics, relevance of animal models, characteristics of safety findings and uncertainties in estimation of MABEL, PAD and human exposure.

citations.quote: In order to further limit the potential for adverse reactions in humans, safety factors are generally applied in the calculation of the starting dose in humans.

cases.question: What is sentinel dosing in early clinical trials?

statements.text: Sentinel dosing is an approach in which the administration of the first dose in any cohort is designed so that a single subject receives a single dose of the active investigational medicinal product (IMP).

citations.quote: It is considered appropriate to design the administration of the first dose in any cohort so that a single subject receives a single dose of the active IMP (often known as sentinel dosing).

statements.text: When placebo is used, sentinel dosing can mean dosing one subject on active and one on placebo simultaneously prior to dosing the remaining subjects in the cohort.

citations.quote: When the study design includes the use of placebo it would be appropriate to allow for one subject on active and one on placebo to be dosed simultaneously prior to dosing the remaining subjects in the cohort.

statements.text: The purpose of sentinel dosing is to reduce the risks associated with exposing all subjects in a cohort simultaneously.

citations.quote: This approach is expected for all single and multiple dosing cohorts, in order to reduce the risks associated with exposing all subjects in a cohort simultaneously.

statements.text: Flexibility to deviate from sentinel dosing is allowed but must be on a risk-proportionate basis with a clear scientific rationale.

citations.quote: Flexibility in this approach is allowed but should be on a risk-proportionate basis with a clear scientific rationale for any proposals not to use this strategy.

statements.text: There should be an adequate period of time between dosing the sentinel subject(s) and the remaining subjects to observe for reactions and adverse events, with the duration depending on the PK and PD characteristics and level of uncertainty associated with the product.

citations.quote: There should be an adequate period of time between the administration of treatment to these first subjects in a cohort and the remaining subjects in the cohort to observe for any reactions and adverse events.
The duration of the interval of observation will depend on the PK and PD characteristics and the level of uncertainty associated with the product (see section 4).

statements.text: After the sentinel observation period, a clearly defined review of all available data for the sentinel subjects should be performed before dosing further subjects in the cohort, with dose stopping rules in place to prevent further dosing if any rule is met.

citations.quote: At the end of the observation period, there should be a clearly defined review of all available data for the sentinel subjects before dosing of further subjects in the cohort, with dose stopping rules in place to prevent further dosing if any rule is met (see also section 8.2.10).

cases.question: On what basis should regions or subpopulations be pooled in a multi-regional clinical trial?

statements.text: Pooling should be based on similarities in intrinsic and/or extrinsic factors relevant to the disease and/or drug.

citations.quote: The pooling strategy should be justified based on the distribution of the intrinsic and extrinsic factors known to affect the treatment response, and the disease under investigation and similarity of those factors across regions.

statements.text: Ethnicity crossing regional boundaries is an important reason to pool subpopulations (for example, Hispanics across the Americas or Caucasians in Europe and North America).

citations.quote: Ethnicity usually crosses regional boundaries and can be an important risk factor for the disease or related to treatment response (as the example in Section 2.2.1. Figure 2b illustrates). Pooling ethnic subpopulations across regions in an MRCT provides an opportunity to evaluate the impact of ethnicity on treatment effects. Examples include Hispanics living in North and South America, or Caucasians living in Europe and North America.

statements.text: Pooling may also be considered by other intrinsic factors such as genotype when members share one or more intrinsic or extrinsic factors important for the drug development programme.

citations.quote: Pooling across regional boundaries by other intrinsic or extrinsic factors may also be considered (e.g., by genotype).

Pooled subpopulations: Pooling a subset of the subjects from a particular region with similarly defined subsets from other regions whose members share one or more intrinsic or extrinsic factors important for the drug development programme at the planning stage.

statements.text: Pooling should be pre-specified at the planning stage when regions or subpopulations are thought to be similar enough with respect to relevant intrinsic and/or extrinsic factors.

citations.quote: Pre-specified pooling of regions or subpopulations, based on established knowledge about similarities, may help provide flexibility in sample size allocation to regions, facilitate the assessment of consistency in treatment effects across regions, and support regulatory decision-making.

Pooled regions: Pooling some geographical regions, countries or regulatory regions at the planning stage, if subjects in those regions are thought to be similar enough with respect to intrinsic and/or extrinsic factors relevant to the disease and/or drug under study.

statements.text: The factors used to define pooling strategies should be collected for enrolled subjects to monitor recruitment and ensure adequate regional and subpopulation representation.

citations.quote: Note that information about the extrinsic and intrinsic factors used to define pooling strategies should be collected for subjects enrolled in the trial to be able to monitor the recruitment strategy and ensure adequate regional and subpopulation representation.

statements.text: Pooling decisions should be reflected in the study protocol and statistical analysis plan and, if stratification by pooled subpopulations is used, the analysis should reflect that pooling.

citations.quote: Pooling strategies should be specified in the study protocol and statistical analysis plan, if applicable.

If some regions were pooled based on intrinsic and/or extrinsic factors, or if pooled subpopulations were defined for stratification purposes during trial planning, then this pooling should be reflected in the analysis.

statements.text: Pooling strategies should be justified scientifically and discussed with relevant regulatory authorities; changes after trial start require justification and regulator discussion to preserve trial integrity.

citations.quote: The pooling strategy should be justified based on the distribution of the intrinsic and extrinsic factors known to affect the treatment response, and the disease under investigation and similarity of those factors across regions.
However, such changes should be justified, discussed with the relevant regulatory authorities, and carried out in a way that preserves trial integrity.

cases.question: What are critical to quality factors in the design of a clinical study?

statements.text: Critical to quality factors are attributes of a study whose integrity is fundamental to the protection of study participants, the reliability and interpretability of the study results, and the decisions made based on the study results.

citations.quote: These critical to quality factors are attributes of a study whose integrity is fundamental to the protection of study participants, the reliability and interpretability of the study results, and the decisions made based on the study results.

statements.text: Critical to quality factors should be identified by the sponsor and other parties designing quality into a clinical study and used to determine risks that threaten their integrity and whether risks should be mitigated.

citations.quote: The sponsor and other parties designing quality into a clinical study should identify the critical to quality factors.

Having identified those factors, it is important to determine the risks that threaten their integrity and decide whether they can be accepted or should be mitigated, based on their probability, detectability and impact.

statements.text: Identification of critical to quality factors should be supported by proactive, crossfunctional discussions and decision making at the time of study planning and engagement of all relevant stakeholders, including patients, is considered during study planning and design.

citations.quote: The identification of critical to quality factors should be supported by proactive, crossfunctional discussions and decision making at the time of study planning
Engagement of all relevant stakeholders, including patients, is considered during study planning and design.

statements.text: Factors to consider when identifying critical to quality factors include that the study objectives address relevant scientific questions, the clinical study design supports a meaningful comparison to the chosen control group, and the number of participants, study duration, and visit frequency are sufficient to support the study objective.

citations.quote: The study objectives address relevant scientific questions appropriate for a given study’s role in the development programme, taking into account the accumulated knowledge about the product.
The clinical study design supports a meaningful comparison of the effects of the drug when compared to the chosen control group.
The number of participants included, the duration of the study, and the frequency of study visits are sufficient to support the study objective.

statements.text: Critical to quality factors include operational feasibility aspects such as availability of qualified investigators and site personnel, availability of required equipment and facilities, availability of the targeted patient population, and ability to enrol and retain a sufficient number of participants.

citations.quote: Feasibility considerations also include but are not limited to regional differences in medical practice and patient populations, the availability of qualified investigators/site personnel with experience in conducting a clinical study (ICH E6), availability of equipment and facilities required to successfully conduct the study, availability of the targeted patient population, and ability to enrol a sufficient number of participants to meet the study objectives.
The retention and follow up of study participants are also key critical to quality factors.

statements.text: Critical to quality factors should be prioritised so they are clear and not cluttered with minor issues, and study procedures should be proportionate to the risks inherent in the study and the importance of the information collected.

citations.quote: The quality factors should be prioritised to identify those that are critical to the study, at the time of the study design, and study procedures should be proportionate to the risks inherent in the study and the importance of the information collected.
The critical to quality factors should be clear and should not be cluttered with minor issues

statements.text: Proactive communication and training about the critical to quality factors and mitigation activities will support understanding of priorities and enhance correct implementation of study protocol, procedures, and operational plans.

citations.quote: Proactive communication of the critical to quality factors and risk mitigation activities will support understanding of priorities and resource allocation by the sponsor and investigator sites.

Proactive support (e.g., training to site staff, relevant to their role, and description of critical to quality factors and potential mitigation measures in the protocol) will enhance correct implementation of study protocol, procedures, and associated operational plans and process design.

statements.text: Critical to quality factors relate to study design elements such as clear predefined objectives, selection of appropriate participants, use of approaches to minimise bias, and well-defined, measurable endpoints that are clinically meaningful and relevant to patients.

citations.quote: the need for clear pre-defined study objectives that address the primary scientific question(s);
selection of appropriate participants that have the disease, condition, or molecular/genetic profile that is being studied;
use of approaches to minimise bias, such as randomisation, blinding or masking, and/or control of confounding;
endpoints that are well-defined, measurable, clinically meaningful, and relevant to patients.

cases.question: How long should the synopsis of a clinical study report usually be?

statements.text: The synopsis of a clinical study report should usually be limited to 3 pages.

citations.quote: A brief synopsis (usually limited to 3 page s) that summarises the study should be provided (see Annex I of the guideline for an example of a synopsis format used in Europe).

cases.question: Who must keep essential records of a clinical trial, and for how long, under ICH GCP E6(R3)?

statements.text: Investigators/institutions should retain the essential records for the required retention period in accordance with applicable regulatory requirements or until the sponsor informs the investigator/institution that these records are no longer needed, whichever is the longest.

citations.quote: The investigator/institution should retain the essential records for the required retention period in accordance with applicable regulatory requirements or until the sponsor informs the investigator/institution that these records are no longer needed, whichever is the longest.

statements.text: Sponsors should obtain agreement from investigators/institutions (and, where applicable, service providers) to retain the essential records for the required retention period in accordance with applicable regulatory requirements or until the sponsor informs the investigator/institution or, where applicable, the service provider that these records are no longer needed, whichever is longest.

citations.quote: To retain the essential records for the required retention period in accordance with applicable regulatory requirements or until the sponsor informs the investigator/institution or, where applicable, the service provider that these records are no longer needed, whichever is longest;

statements.text: The sponsor (or subsequent owners of the data) should retain the sponsor-specific essential records pertaining to the trial in accordance with the applicable regulatory requirement(s).

citations.quote: The sponsor (or subsequent owners of the data) should retain the sponsor-specific essential records pertaining to the trial in accordance with the applicable regulatory requirement(s)

statements.text: The sponsor should inform the investigator(s)/institution(s) and service providers, when appropriate, in writing of the requirements for the retention of essential records and should notify the investigator(s)/institution(s) and service providers, when appropriate, in writing when the trial-related records are no longer needed in accordance with applicable regulatory requirements.

citations.quote: The sponsor should inform the investigator(s)/institution(s) and service providers, when appropriate, in writing of the requirements for the retention of essential records and should notify the investigator(s)/institution(s) and service providers, when appropriate, in writing when the trial-related records are no longer needed in accordance with applicable regulatory requirements.

statements.text: Certain trial materials (e.g., investigational product samples) should be retained either until the analyses of the trial data are complete or as required by the applicable regulatory requirement(s), whichever represents the longer retention period.

citations.quote: The samples should be retained either until the analyses of the trial data are complete or as required by the applicable regulatory requirement(s), whichever represents the longer retention period.

statements.text: Essential records should be retained securely by sponsors and investigators for the required period in accordance with applicable regulatory requirements and be available to regulatory authorities, monitors, auditors and IRBs/IECs (as appropriate) upon request.

citations.quote: Essential records should be retained securely by sponsors and investigators for the required period in accordance with applicable regulatory requirements.

These essential records should be available to regulatory authorities, monitors, auditors and IRBs/IECs (as appropriate) upon request to enable appropriate evaluation of the trial conduct in order to ensure the reliability of trial results.

statements.text: The investigator/institution should have access to and the ability to maintain the essential records generated by the investigator/institution before and during the conduct of the trial and retain them in accordance with applicable regulatory requirements.

citations.quote: The investigator/institution should have access to and the ability to maintain the essential records generated by the investigator/institution before and during the conduct of the trial and retain them in accordance with applicable regulatory requirements.

statements.text: If sponsor-held essential records (e.g., SUSAR reports) are accessed by the investigator via a sponsor-provided portal, those essential records would need to be retained by the investigator/institution at the end of the trial.

citations.quote: For example, the investigator may access relevant essential records from the sponsor (e.g., suspected unexpected serious adverse reactions (SUSAR) reports) via a sponsorprovided portal, and these essential records would need to be retained by the investigator/institution at the end of the trial.

statements.text: For some trial records listed in the Essential Record Table, if these trial records are produced, they are considered essential and should be retained.

citations.quote: If these trial records are produced, they are considered essential and should be retained (see sections C3.1 and C3.2).

cases.question: How should computerised systems used in clinical trials be validated under ICH E6(R3)?

statements.text: The responsible party is responsible for the validation status of the system throughout its life cycle and should base the validation approach on a risk assessment considering intended use, importance of the data and potential to affect participant well‑being and trial reliability.

citations.quote: (a) The responsible party is responsible for the validation status of the system throughout its life cycle. The approach to validation of computerised systems should be based on a risk assessment that considers the intended use of the system; the purpose and importance of the data/record that are collected/generated, maintained and retained in the system; and the potential of the system to affect the well-being, rights and safety of trial participants and the reliability of trial results.

statements.text: Validation should demonstrate that the system conforms to established requirements for completeness, accuracy and reliability and that its performance is consistent with its intended purpose.

citations.quote: (b) Validation should demonstrate that the system conforms to the established requirements for completeness, accuracy and reliability and that its performance is consistent with its intended purpose.

statements.text: Systems should be appropriately validated prior to use and subsequent changes should be validated based on risk, considering both previously collected and new data in line with change control procedures.

citations.quote: (c) Systems should be appropriately validated prior to use. Subsequent changes to the system should be validated based on risk and should consider both previously collected and new data in line with change control procedures.

statements.text: Periodic review may be appropriate to ensure that computerised systems remain in a validated state throughout the life cycle of the system.

citations.quote: (d) Periodic review may be appropriate to ensure that computerised systems remain in a validated state throughout the life cycle of the system.

statements.text: Both standard system functionality and protocol‑specific configurations and customisations, including automated data entry checks and calculations, and interfaces between systems, should be defined and validated; different degrees of validation may be needed depending on system type.

citations.quote: (e) Both standard system functionality and protocol-specific configurations and customisations, including automated data entry checks and calculations, should be validated. Interfaces between systems should also be defined and validated. Different degrees of validation may be needed for bespoke systems, systems designed to be configured or systems where no alterations are needed.

statements.text: Where relevant, validation procedures (until decommissioning) should cover system design, system requirement, functionality testing, configuration, release, setup, installation and change control.

citations.quote: (f) Where relevant, validation procedures (until decommissioning) should cover the following: system design, system requirement, functionality testing, configuration, release, setup, installation and change control.

statements.text: The responsible party should ensure validation documentation is maintained and retained and that systems (including those developed by other parties) are validated as fit for purpose for use in the trial.

citations.quote: (g) The responsible party should ensure that the computerised systems are validated as fit for purpose for use in the trial, including those developed by other parties. They should ensure that validation documentation is maintained and retained.

statements.text: Validation should generally include defining the requirements and specifications for the system and their testing, along with associated documentation, especially for critical functionality such as randomisation, dosing and collection of endpoint data.

citations.quote: (h) Validation should generally include defining the requirements and specifications for the system and their testing, along with the associated documentation, to ensure the system is fit for purpose for use in the trial, especially for critical functionality, such as randomisation, dosing and dose titrations and reductions, and collection of endpoint data.

statements.text: Computerised systems used in clinical trials should be fit for purpose (e.g., through risk‑based validation, if appropriate) and address factors critical to their quality in their design or adaptation to ensure data integrity.

citations.quote: 9.3 Computerised systems used in clinical trials should be fit for purpose (e.g., through risk-based validation, if appropriate), and factors critical to their quality should be addressed in their design or adaptation for clinical trial purposes to ensure the integrity of relevant trial data.

statements.text: At the point of data capture, automated data validation checks to raise data queries should be considered as required based on risk, and their implementation should be controlled and documented.

citations.quote: (c) At the point of data capture, automated data validation checks to raise data queries should be considered as required based on risk, and their implementation should be controlled and documented.

statements.text: Validated processes and/or appropriate processes such as reconciliation should be in place to ensure electronic data (including relevant metadata) transferred between computerised systems retains its integrity and preserves its confidentiality; the data exchange/transfer process or system migration should be documented to ensure traceability.

citations.quote: Validated processes and/or other appropriate processes such as reconciliation should be in place to ensure that electronic data, including relevant metadata, transferred between computerised systems retains its integrity and preserves its confidentiality.

The data exchange/transfer process or system migration should be documented to ensure traceability, and data reconciliation should be implemented as appropriate to avoid data loss and unintended modifications.

statements.text: The approach to implementing, evaluating, accessing, managing and reviewing metadata for higher‑criticality data should ensure audit trails and logs are maintained, not disabled or modified except in rare circumstances with justification, and are interpretable and reviewable.

citations.quote: (b) Ensuring that audit trails, reports and logs are not disabled. Audit trails should not be modified except in rare circumstances (e.g., when a participant’s personal information is inadvertently included in the data) and only if a log of such action and justification is maintained;
(c) Ensuring that audit trails and logs are interpretable and can support review;

statements.text: When using sponsor‑deployed computerised systems the sponsor should have a record of important systems including their validation status, ensure requirements such as validation, audit trails, user management, backup and IT security are addressed and implemented, and maintain records of authorised users and access permissions.

citations.quote: (x)(i) Have a record of the important computerised systems used in a clinical trial. This should include the use, functionality, interfaces and validation status of each computerised system, and who is responsible for its management should be described.

(x)(ii) Ensure that the requirements for computerised systems (e.g., requirements for validation, audit trails, user management, backup, disaster recovery and IT security) are addressed and implemented and that documented procedures and adequate training are in place to ensure the correct development, maintenance and use of computerised systems in clinical trials (see section 4).
(x)(iii) Maintain a record of the individual users who are authorised to access the system, their roles and their access permissions;

cases.question: How formal should a quality risk management process be under ICH Q9(R1)?

statements.text: ICH Q9(R1) says formality in quality risk management is a continuum, not a binary choice.

citations.quote: Formality in quality risk management is not a binary concept (i.e. formal/informal); varying degrees of formality may be applied during quality risk management activities, including when making risk-based decisions. In this way, formality can be considered a continuum (or spectrum), ranging from low to high.

statements.text: The level of formality applied should be commensurate with the level of risk, effort and documentation needed.

citations.quote: The level of effort, formality and documentation of the quality risk management process should be commensurate with the level of risk.

statements.text: When determining how much formality to apply, ICH Q9(R1) lists uncertainty, importance and complexity as factors to consider.

citations.quote: When determining how much formality to apply to a given quality risk management activity, certain factors may be considered. These may include, for example, the following: • Uncertainty: ... • Importance: ... • Complexity: ...

statements.text: Higher levels of uncertainty, importance or complexity may require more formal quality risk management approaches.

citations.quote: Higher levels of uncertainty, importance or complexity may require more formal quality risk management approaches to manage potential risks and to support effective risk-based decisionmaking.

statements.text: ICH Q9(R1) describes characteristics of higher formality such as explicitly performing all parts of the QRM process, generating stand-alone QRM reports, using QRM tools, assembling cross-functional teams and possibly using a facilitator.

citations.quote: All parts of the quality risk management process (risk assessment, risk control, risk review and risk communication) are explicitly performed, and stand-alone quality risk management reports or related documents which address all aspects of the process may be generated and are documented (e.g., within the quality system).
Quality risk management tools, including those shown in Annex 1, are used in some or all parts of the process.
A cross-functional team is assembled for the quality risk management activity.
Use of a facilitator, with experience and knowledge of the quality risk management process, may be integral to a higher formality process.

statements.text: ICH Q9(R1) also describes characteristics of lower formality such as embedding risk activities within other quality system elements, not using tools, not requiring cross-functional teams and not generating stand-alone reports.

citations.quote: One or more parts of the quality risk management process are not performed as standalone activities but are addressed within other elements of the quality system which may have risk assessment and risk control activities embedded within them.
Quality risk management tools might not be used in some or all parts of the process.
A cross-functional team might not be necessary.
Stand-alone quality risk management reports might not be generated. The outcome of the quality risk management process is usually documented in the relevant parts of the quality system.

statements.text: The overall approach for determining formality should be described within the quality system and resource constraints should not justify lower formality.

citations.quote: The overall approach for determining how much formality to apply during quality risk management activities should be described within the quality system.
Resource constraints should not be used to justify the use of lower levels of formality in the quality risk management process.

statements.text: ICH Q9(R1) links appropriate use of QRM to efficient resource use but clarifies QRM does not replace regulatory obligations and must not be used to justify otherwise unacceptable practices.

citations.quote: An understanding of formality in quality risk management may lead to resources being used more efficiently, where lower risk issues are dealt with via less formal means, freeing up resources for managing higher risk issues and more complex problems that may require increased levels of rigor and effort.
Quality risk management should not be used in a manner where decisions are made that justify a practice that would otherwise, in accordance with regulations and/or guidance, be deemed unacceptable.

cases.question: When may a short form written consent document be used in an FDA-regulated clinical investigation?

statements.text: A short form may be used when the elements of informed consent required by 21 CFR 50.25 are presented orally to the subject or the subject’s legally authorized representative (LAR).

citations.quote: An IRB may approve a short form to be used in appropriate situations where the elements of informed consent required by 21 CFR 50.25 are presented orally to the subject or the subject’s LAR (21 CFR 50.27(b)(2)).

statements.text: IRBs may consider approving a short form in situations where the subject or the subject’s LAR is unable to read due to low literacy or visual impairment.

citations.quote: For example, IRBs may consider approving the use of a short form in situations where the subject or the subject’s LAR is unable to read due to low literacy or visual impairment.52

statements.text: Use of the short form requires that there be a witness to the oral presentation of information to the subject or the subject’s LAR.

citations.quote: Use of the short form requires that there be a witness to the oral presentation of information to the subject or the subject's LAR (21 CFR 50.27(b)(2)).

statements.text: When the short form is used, the IRB is required to approve a written summary of the information to be presented orally and a copy of the short form and the written summary must be given to the person signing the form.

citations.quote: When the short form is used, the IRB is required to approve a written summary of the information to be presented orally (21 CFR 50.27(b)(2)).
A copy of the short form and the written summary must be given to the person signing the form (that is, the subject or the subject’s LAR) (21 CFR 50.27(b)(2)).

statements.text: Only the short form itself is to be signed by the subject or the representative; the witness signs both the short form and a copy of the summary, and the person actually obtaining consent signs a copy of the summary.

citations.quote: Only the short form itself is to be signed by the subject or the representative.
However, the witness shall sign both the short form and a copy of the summary, and the person actually obtaining the consent shall sign a copy of the summary.

the acceptance criteria for C max can be widened to a maximum of 69.84 – 143.19%.

cases.question: What do FDA's Part 11 guidance and EU GMP Annex 11 each say about audit trails?

citations.quote: Consideration should be given, based on a risk assessment, to building into the system the creation of a record of all GMP-relevant changes and deletions (a system generated "audit trail"). For change or deletion of GMP-relevant data the reason should be documented. Audit trails need to be available and convertible to a generally intelligible form and regularly reviewed.

statements.text: FDA 2003 Part 11 guidance: FDA stated it "intends to exercise enforcement discretion with respect to computer-generated, time-stamped audit trails" while nevertheless requiring compliance with applicable predicate rule documentation requirements and protections so that "changes to records do not obscure previous entries."

citations.quote: The Agency intends to exercise enforcement discretion regarding specific part 11 requirements related to computer- generated, time-stamped audit trails (§ 11.10 (e), (k)(2) and any corresponding requirement in §11.30). Persons must still comply with all applicable predicate rule requirements related to documentation of, for example, date (e.g., § 58.130(e)), time, or sequencing of events, as well as any requirements for ensuring t hat changes to records do not obscure previous entries.

statements.text: FDA 2003 Part 11 guidance: FDA recommended basing the decision on whether to apply audit trails on the need to comply with predicate rules, a "justified and documented risk assessment," and the potential effect on product quality and safety and record integrity.

citations.quote: We recommend that you base your decision on whether to apply audit trails, or other appropriate measures, on the need to comply with p redicate rule requirements, a justified and documented risk assessment, and a determination of the potential effect on product quality and safety and record integrity.

statements.text: FDA 2024 guidance: FDA recommends that audit trails be retained in a format that is searchable and sortable, or if not practical retained in a static format (e.g., PDFs) that clearly correspond to the respective data elements and/or records.

citations.quote: FDA recommends that the audit trail be retained in a format that is searchable and sortable. If this is not practical, audit trail files should be retained in a static format (e.g., PDFs) and clearly correspond to the respective data elements and/or records (see Q3 on certified copies).

statements.text: FDA 2024 guidance: The audit trail components must include the date and time the data element or information was entered or modified, the individual making the change (e.g., user ID and user role), and the old value and the new value; the audit trail "should include the reason for the change if applicable."

citations.quote: The information should be complete and understandable with clear and concise terms to describe the components of the audit trail. Audit trail components must include (1) the date and time the data element or information was entered or modified (see Q14), (2) the individual making the change (e.g., user ID and user role), and (3) the old value and the new value.59 The audit trail should include the reason for the change if applicable.

statements.text: FDA 2024 guidance: Audit trail documentation must be retained for a period at least as long as the period required for the subject electronic records and must be available for FDA review and copying.

citations.quote: Audit trail documentation must be retained for a period at least as long as the period required for the subject electronic records and must be available for FDA review and copying (see §§ 11.10(e) and 11.30).

statements.text: FDA 2024 guidance: Audit trails should be protected from modification and from being disabled, record changes must not obscure previously recorded information, periodic review may be helpful and the decision to review should be based on a risk assessment, and all audit trail documentation must be available for FDA inspection.

citations.quote:
Record changes must not obscure previously recorded information.56
To ensure the trustworthiness and reliability of electronic records, audit trails must capture electronic record activities including all changes made to the electronic record, the individuals making the changes, and the date and time of the changes57 and should include the reasons for the changes. Audit trails should be protected from modification and from being disabled.
Periodic review of the audit trail may be helpful for sponsors to ensure data quality, authenticity, and integrity. The decision to review audit trails should be based on a risk assessment of the clinical investigation, considering the systems, procedures, and controls in place.
All audit trail documentation on the creation, modification, and deletion of electronic records must be available for FDA inspection.58

statements.text: FDA (both 2003 and 2024): FDA reiterates that even where there are no predicate rule requirements, it may nonetheless be important to have audit trails or other measures in place and recommends basing the decision on predicate rule needs, a documented risk assessment, and potential effects on record integrity.

citations.quote: Even if there are no predicate rule requirements to document, for example, date, time, or sequence of events in a particular instance, it may nonetheless be important to have audit trails or other physical, logical, or procedural security measures in place to ensure the trustworthiness and reliability of the records.

The 2003 part 11 guidance states that FDA intends to exercise enforcement discretion with respect to specific part 11 requirements, including but not limited to computer-generated, timestamped audit trails.60 Persons must still comply with all applicable predicate rules. Even where there are no predicate rule requirements related to documentation, it is nonetheless important to have audit trails or other physical, logical, or procedural security measures in place to ensure the trustworthiness and reliability of the electronic records (see Q11). FDA recommends basing a decision regarding whether to apply audit trails or other appropriate measures on the need to comply with predicate rule requirements, a justified and documented risk assessment, and a determination of the potential effect on record integrity.

cases.question: How do FDA and the EMA approach multiplicity adjustment when a trial tests several hypotheses?

statements.text: FDA: multiplicity arises when multiple facets (doses, time points, subgroups) are analyzed because it can inflate the Type I error rate and make conclusions unreliable.

citations.quote: Even when a single outcome variable is being assessed, if multiple facets of that outcome are analyzed (e.g., multiple dose groups, multiple time points, or multiple subject subgroups based on demographic or other characteristics) and if any one of the analyses is used to conclude that the drug has been shown to produce a beneficial effect, the multiplicity of analyses may cause inflation of the Type I error rate.

statements.text: FDA: sponsors should prospectively specify all planned endpoints, time points, analysis populations, doses, and analyses and select prespecified multiplicity adjustments as appropriate.

citations.quote: For controlling multiplicity, an important principle is to first prospectively specify all planned endpoints, time points, analysis populations, doses, and analyses; then, once these factors are specified, appropriate adjustments for multiple endpoints and analyses can be selected, prespecified, and applied, as appropriate.

statements.text: FDA: the guidance focuses on controlling the Type I error rate for the prespecified set of endpoints so that major findings are well supported and descriptive analyses (e.g., subgroup or time-of-onset) are considered descriptive and can be included in labeling without p-values.

citations.quote: A focus of this guidance is control of the Type I error rate for the prespecified set of endpoints (i.e., primary and secondary endpoints) of a clinical trial to ensure that the major findings of a clinical trial are well supported, and the effects of the drug have been demonstrated.

Analyses that explicate the characteristics of an effect on an endpoint that has been demonstrated—such as time of onset, distribution of effect sizes across the population, effects in subgroups, and effects on the components of a composite endpoint—are all descriptive to provide a deeper understanding of the nature of that endpoint finding, and do not extend to effects outside of that endpoint. These descriptive analyses can be considered for inclusion in the FDA-approved labeling without presenting p-values.

statements.text: FDA: the overall Type I error rate is typically held to 0.05 (or 0.025 for one-sided tests) and various methods (e.g., Bonferroni, Holm, Hochberg, graphical methods) can be used to control multiplicity.

citations.quote: This error rate is typically held to 0.05 (or 0.025 for one-sided tests).

Examples include the Bonferroni, Holm (Holm 1979), and Hochberg (Hochberg 1988) procedures, which do not assume any hierarchy among the tested null hypotheses... Other viable methods apply a combination of partial alpha allocation and hierarchies, such as graphical methods (Bretz et al. 2009) that are presented in the appendix.

statements.text: FDA: when a primary endpoint is tested for non-inferiority and then for superiority, no multiplicity adjustment is needed if that endpoint alone is tested, but if additional endpoints are tested multiplicity adjustments or ordered testing/alpha allocation should be used.

citations.quote: If this endpoint is the only endpoint being tested, then noninferiority and superiority can be tested without multiplicity adjustment because the null hypotheses of non-inferiority and superiority are naturally ordered, and the two tests apply to the one hierarchy considered for this endpoint.
However, if at least one more endpoint is included for testing, then multiplicity issues arise, and adjustments should be made to control the overall Type I error probability.

statements.text: EMA/CPMP: a simple trial with two treatment groups, a single primary variable and one pre-specified null hypothesis requires no adjustment of the type I error.

citations.quote: A clinical study that requires no adjustment of th e type I error is one that consists of two treatment groups, that uses a single primary va riable, and has a confirmatory statistical strategy that pre-specifies just one single null hypothesis relating to the primary variable and no interim analysis.

statements.text: EMA/CPMP: when multiple primary variables are required to define clinically relevant benefit, statistical significance is needed for all primary variables and "no formal adjustment is necessary" (but sample size must account for inflated type II error).

citations.quote: Statistical significance is needed for all primary variables. Therefore, no formal adjustment is necessary.

This procedure inflates the relevant type II error (here: falsely accepting that at least one null hypothesis is true), which in the worst case scenario is the sum of the type II errors connected with the individual hypotheses. Th is inflation must be taken into account for a proper estimation of the sample size for the trial.

statements.text: EMA/CPMP: alternative methods that control family-wise error (closed testing procedures) can avoid formal type I adjustment while allowing clinical interpretation; the preferred multiple-level-α-test should be pre-defined and detailed in protocol or SAP, and if an unforeseen multiple test occurs a conservative approach (e.g., Bonferroni) is necessary.

citations.quote: The methods de scribed allow clinical interpretation, deal satisfactorily with the issue of multiplicity but avoid the need for any formal adjustment of type I error rates. Indeed the methods are memb ers from the set of closed testing procedures that control the family-wise error rate.
Because alternative methods to deal correctly with multiplicity are often available which may lead to different conclusions, pre-definition of the preferred multiple-level-α -test is necessary.
To avoid problems in interpretation, details of the procedure should be contained in the study protocol or the statistical analysis plan.
If a multiple test situation occurs which was not foreseen, a conservative approach will be necessary e.g. Bonferroni’s or a related proce dure.

statements.text: ICH E9: when multiplicity is present adjustment should be considered, and remaining multiplicity after reducing steps should be identified in the protocol with details or justification in the analysis plan.

citations.quote: When multiplicity is present, the usual frequentist approach to the analysis of clinical trial data may necessitate an adjustment to the type I error.

In confirmatory analyses, any aspects of multiplicity which remain after steps of this kind have been taken should be identified in the protocol; adjustment should always be considered and the details of any adjustment procedure or an explanation of why adjustment is not thought to be necessary should be set out in the analysis plan.

cases.question: A generic product's Cmax turns out to be highly variable. How far could the EU widen the acceptance limits, and at what within-subject standard deviation of the reference does the FDA switch from the usual two one-sided tests to reference scaling?

statements.text: Under the EMA guideline, the acceptance criteria for Cmax can be widened up to 69.84 – 143.19% for highly variable drugs when within-subject variability for Cmax of the reference is >30%.

statements.text: EMA CHMP guideline (adjustment for baseline covariates): "The stratification variables used for randomisation should be adjusted for in the primary analysis."

citations.quote: The stratification variables used for randomisation should be adjusted for in the primary analysis.

statements.text: EMA CHMP guideline (stratification): "stratification variables, if not solely used for administrative reasons, should usually be included as covariates or stratification variables in the primary analysis regardless of their prognostic value."

citations.quote: stratification variables, if not solely used for administrative reasons, should usually be included as covariates or stratification variables in the primary analysis regardless of their prognostic value.

statements.text: ICH E9(R1): The "treatment policy strategy" addresses an intercurrent event by analysing outcomes regardless of the intercurrent event (analysis aligned with a treatment policy strategy).

statements.text: ICH E9(R1): The "while on treatment strategy" restricts the observation time of interest to the time before the intercurrent event (e.g. "while alive" when death is the intercurrent event).

citations.quote: Like the composite variable strategy, the while on treatment strategy can hence be thought of as impacting the definition of the variable, in this case by restricting the observation time of interest to the time before the intercurrent event.
Terminology for this strategy will depend on the intercurrent event of interest ; e.g. “while alive”, when considering death as an intercurrent event.

statements.text: ICH E9(R1): The "principal stratum strategy" defines the target population as a principal stratum in which the intercurrent event would or would not occur and estimates treatment effect within that stratum.

citations.quote: The target population might be taken to be the “ principal stratum” (see Glossary) in which an intercurrent event would occur . Alternatively, the target population might be taken to be the principal stratum in which an intercurrent event would not occur. The clinical question of interest relates to the treatment effect only within the principal stratum.

statements.text: ICH E9(R1): The estimand and chosen strategy must consider interpretability and plausibility of assumptions (for example, justification of hypothetical conditions and implications of discontinuation for tolerability).

citations.quote: The hypothetical conditions described should therefore be justified for the quantification of an interpretable treatment effect that is relevant to inform the decisions to be taken by regulators, and use of the medicine in clinical practice.

A clinical question of interest based on the effect if all subjects had been able to continue with treatment is not well-defined without a thorough discussion of the hypothetical conditions under whic h it is supposed that they would have continued. T he inability to tolerate a treatment may constitute, in itself, evidence of an inability to achieve a favourable outcome.

statements.text: ICH E9(R1): When using treatment-policy or hypothetical strategies, practical estimation considerations differ (e.g. missing data when observation is terminated after an intercurrent event may make treatment-policy assumptions implausible and require sensitivity analyses).

citations.quote: When most subjects are followed-up even after the respective intercurrent event (e.g. discontinuation of treatment), the remaining problem of missing data may be relatively minor. In contrast, when observation is terminated after an intercurrent event, which is obviously undesirable in respect of this strategy, the assumption that (unobserved) outcomes for discontinuing subjects are similar to the (observed) outcomes for those who remain on treatment will often be implausible. An alternative approach to handle the missing data would need to be justified and sensitivity analysis will be expected.

cases.question: Once the primary endpoint has been met, under what conditions can secondary endpoints support an additional claim according to both the EMA multiplicity points to consider and the FDA multiple endpoints guidance?

statements.text: Both EMA and FDA say an effect on secondary endpoints can be considered for an additional claim only after the primary objective/endpoint has been achieved.

citations.quote: Significant effects in these variables can be considered for an additional claim only after the primary objective of the clinical trial has been achieved, and if they were part of the confirmatory strategy
When an effect on the primary endpoint is shown, the secondary endpoints can be formally tested.

statements.text: EMA requires the secondary variables to have been pre-specified and part of an appropriately planned statistical analysis strategy for additional claims.

citations.quote: Additional claims on statistically significant and clinically relevant findings based on secondary variables or on subgroups are possible only after the primary objective of the clinical trial has been achieved, and if the respective questions were pre-specified, and were part of an appropriately planned statistical analysis strategy.

statements.text: EMA endorses a hierarchical procedure: after rejecting the primary null hypothesis, further confirmatory tests on secondary variables can be performed in a further hierarchical order.

citations.quote: Once the null hypothesis concerning the primary objective is rejected (and the primary objective thus established), further confirmatory statistical tests on secondary variables can be performed using a further hierarchical order for the secondary variables themselves if there is more than one.

statements.text: FDA similarly advises grouping endpoints hierarchically and that secondary endpoints can be tested to demonstrate additional clinically important effects.

citations.quote: Endpoints in adequate and well-controlled drug trials are usually grouped hierarchically, often according to their clinical importance... Secondary endpoints can provide useful description to support the primary endpoint(s) and/or demonstrate additional clinically important effects.

statements.text: FDA advises that secondary endpoints that could provide evidence of additional effects should be included in the Type I error control plan, and that limiting the number of secondary endpoints is desirable because multiplicity adjustments reduce power.

citations.quote: As a general principle, it is important to include the secondary endpoints that can potentially provide evidence of additional effects of the drug on the disease or condition in the Type I error control plan.

In general, it may be desirable to limit the number of secondary endpoints, because if multiplicity adjustments are used, the chance of demonstrating an effect on any secondary endpoint may become increasingly small as the number of secondary endpoints increases

statements.text: FDA states exploratory endpoints do not need multiplicity adjustment because they are generally not used to support conclusions.

citations.quote: Exploratory endpoints do not need multiplicity adjustment because they are generally not used to support conclusions.

statements.text: EMA warns that changes in secondary variables that are a direct consequence of changes in the primary variable cannot be the basis for a separate labeling claim.

citations.quote: It is of note to mention that changes in secondary variables that are considered a direct consequence of the respective changes in the primary variables cannot be part of the labelling claims.

statements.text: EMA requires that the statistical procedures to deal with multiplicity be fully detailed in the study protocol or statistical analysis plan to allow assessment of suitability and appropriateness.

citations.quote: It is therefore necessary that the statistical procedures planned to deal with, or to avoid, multiplicity are fully detailed in the study protocol or in the statistical analysis plan to allow an assessment of their suitability and appropriateness.

statements.text: FDA notes that when non-inferiority and superiority (or multiple endpoint tests) are present, multiplicity issues arise and appropriate control (for example hierarchy or alpha allocation) should be used.

citations.quote: If this endpoint is the only endpoint being tested, then noninferiority and superiority can be tested without multiplicity adjustment because the null hypotheses of non-inferiority and superiority are naturally ordered... However, if at least one more endpoint is included for testing, then multiplicity issues arise, and adjustments should be made to control the overall Type I error probability.
There should be appropriate control in some manner (e.g., test the secondary endpoint only if the primary endpoint superiority is shown or split alpha between the two tests).

cases.question: Why must an adaptive trial design address inflation of false-positive conclusions, and how can the sponsor demonstrate control when no analytical formula is available?

statements.text: An adaptive design must address the possibility of Type I error inflation because adaptive features can increase the chance of false positive conclusions (Type I error) beyond the nominal level.

citations.quote: Adaptive design proposals for trials incorporating null hypothesis testing should therefore address the possibility of Type I error probability inflation.

If each of these two tests were performed at the conventional .025 one-sided significance level and the drug were not effective, the overall chance of the trial yielding a Type I error would exceed 2.5 percent.

statements.text: Adaptive features other than explicit multiple testing (for example, naive population selection) can also inflate Type I error and lead to erroneous conclusions, so sponsors must consider these risks.

citations.quote: Explicit multiple hypothesis tests are not the only way adaptive design features can lead to erroneous conclusions.

If the final analysis is performed in the selected population at a .025 significance level and includes the same data that were used to choose the patient population, the Type I error probability would exceed 2.5 percent.

statements.text: When no analytical formula or tractable distribution is available, the sponsor can use clinical trial simulations to estimate operating characteristics including Type I error probability by simulating many instances of the trial under null-hypothesis scenarios and evaluating the proportion of simulated trials that lead to a false positive conclusion.

citations.quote: For some adaptive designs, however, it either is not possible to derive relevant distributions of test statistics, or the distributions themselves are not computationally tractable... In these cases, trial operating characteristics can often be estimated by means of clinical trial simulations.

For simulations intended to estimate Type I error probability, hypothetical clinical trials would be simulated under a series of assumptions compatible with the null hypothesis. For each set of such assumptions, the proportion of simulated trials that led to a false positive conclusion would be taken as an estimate of Type I error probability under those assumptions.

statements.text: Choosing which null scenarios to simulate should combine medical and mathematical considerations and may require exploring nuisance parameters and a grid of plausible values to cover the plausible range.

citations.quote: Identifying which scenarios should be considered when estimating Type I error probability can be challenging and may rely on a combination of medical and mathematical considerations.

It is common to perform simulations on a grid of plausible values and argue based on the totality of the evidence from the simulations that maximal Type I error probability likely does not exceed a desired level across the range covered by the grid.

statements.text: Sponsors should use sufficiently many simulation iterations to ensure the precision of the Type I error estimate (for example, 100,000 iterations giving a 95% confidence interval width of approximately ± 0.1%), though fewer iterations (for example, 10,000) may suffice in some circumstances.

citations.quote: Using 100,000 iterations per scenario, for instance, ensures a 95% confidence interval for estimated Type I error probability with a width of approximately ± 0.1%, which would be sufficient in most cases.
For example, it might be sufficient to use 10,000 iterations if a particularly fine grid of scenarios is explored and every scenario has an estimated Type I error probability below the desired level.

statements.text: Simulations should be designed carefully (for example, using different random seeds across scenarios) and the sponsor should evaluate operating characteristics such as power, expected sample size, and bias as appropriate.

citations.quote: In general, it is also preferable to use different random seeds for different simulation scenarios; this helps avoid consistently atypical results across scenarios.

Clinical trial simulations can also be used to estimate power and other relevant operating characteristics, such as expected sample size, expected duration, and bias in treatment effect estimates, for complex adaptive designs.

statements.text: For bioequivalence or other regulatory submissions, sponsors should prespecify adaptive design details before study initiation and may support their approach with published validation or simulation results showing that the Type I error probability is controlled at an acceptable nominal level (for example, 0.05).

citations.quote: The details of the adaptive design should be completely specified prior to initiation of the study and documented accordingly.

Support might include published literature in peer-reviewed journals in which the applicant’s proposed approach is validated or simulation results that meet desired criteria (e.g., the Type I error probability of the proposed approach is controlled at a nominal level of 0.05 for a BE test).

statements.text: For complex designs combining multiple adaptive features, the same principles apply but simulations will often be critical because estimating Type I error probability is particularly difficult.

citations.quote: It may be particularly difficult to estimate Type I error probability and other operating characteristics for designs that incorporate multiple adaptive features. Clinical trial simulations (section VI.A.) will often be critical to evaluate the trial design.

cases.question: Line up the standard 15-day reporting clocks: serious unexpected reactions that are not fatal under ICH E2A, IND safety reports to the FDA, and serious individual case reports in the EU under GVP Module VI.

statements.text: ICH E2A (1994) sets the 15-day clock from the sponsor’s first knowledge: “...must be filed as soon as possible but no later than 15 calendar days after first knowledge by the sponsor that the case meets the minimum criteria for expedited reporting.”

citations.quote: Serious, unexpected reactions (ADRs) that are not fatal or life-threatening must be filed as soon as possible but no later than 15 calendar days after first knowledge by the sponsor that the case meets the minimum criteria for expedited reporting.

statements.text: FDA IND safety-reporting requires notification “as soon as possible but no later than 15 calendar days after the sponsor determines that the information qualifies for reporting in an IND safety report.”

citations.quote: Under § 312.32(c), the sponsor is required to notify FDA and all participating investigators through an IND safety report of potential serious risks from clinical trials or any other source as soon as possible but no later than 15 calendar days after the sponsor determines that the information qualifies for reporting in an IND safety report.

statements.text: FDA clarifies day zero for 15-day IND reports as either the day the sponsor initially receives a single, interpretable case or the day the sponsor determines that multiple cases qualify for expedited reporting: “Day zero for 7- and 15-day reports is considered as (1) the day the sponsor initially receives information for a case that is interpretable as a single case or (2) the day the sponsor determines that multiple cases qualify for expedited reporting.”

citations.quote: Day zero for 7- and 15-day reports is considered as (1) the day the sponsor initially receives information for a case that is interpretable as a single case or (2) the day the sponsor determines that multiple cases qualify for expedited reporting.

statements.text: EU GVP Module VI requires serious valid ICSRs to be submitted “as soon as possible, but in no case later than 15 calendar days after initial receipt of the information by the national or regional pharmacovigilance centre ... or by any personnel of the marketing authorisation holder”: the clock runs from initial receipt by the competent centre or MAH personnel.

citations.quote: In general, the submission of serious valid ICSRs is required as soon as possible, but in no case later than 15 calendar days after initial receipt of the information by the national or regional pharmacovigilance centre of a competent authority or by any personnel of the marketing authorisation holder, including medical representatives and contractors.
